units.text: INT. HUSBAND - CONTINUOUS
It is always worth while asking a question, though it is not always worth while answering one.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Enter MASON.
Is Mr. Trafford in his room?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Yes, Sir Robert.
units.name: MASON

units.text: Puts what he has written into an envelope , which he then carefully closes .
Tell him to have this sent off in cipher at once. There must not be a moment’s delay.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Yes, Sir Robert.
units.name: MASON

units.text: Oh! just give that back to me again.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Writes something on the envelope .
MASON then goes out with the letter .
She must have had some curious hold over Baron Arnheim. I wonder what it was.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Smiling .
I wonder.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: I will fight her to the death, as long as my wife knows nothing.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Strongly .
Oh, fight in any case—in any case.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: With a gesture of despair .

If my wife found out, there would be little left to fight for. Well, as soon as I hear from Vienna, I shall let you know the result. It is a chance, just a chance, but I believe in it. And as I fought the age with its own weapons, I will fight her with her weapons. It is only fair, and she looks like a woman with a past, doesn’t she?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Most pretty women do. But there is a fashion in pasts just as there is a fashion in frocks. Perhaps Mrs. Cheveley’s past is merely a slightly décolleté one, and they are excessively popular nowadays. Besides, my dear Robert, I should not build too high hopes on frightening Mrs. Cheveley. I should not fancy Mrs. Cheveley is a woman who would be easily frightened. She has survived all her creditors, and she shows wonderful presence of mind.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Oh! I live on hopes now. I clutch at every chance. I feel like a man on a ship that is sinking. The water is round my feet, and the very air is bitter with storm. Hush! I hear my wife’s voice.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Enter LADY CHILTERN in walking dress .
Good afternoon, Lord Goring!
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Good afternoon, Lady Chiltern! Have you been in the Park?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: No; I have just come from the Woman’s Liberal Association, where, by the way, Robert, your name was received with loud applause, and now I have come in to have my tea.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: To LORD GORING.
You will wait and have some tea, won’t you?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: I’ll wait for a short time, thanks.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: I will be back in a moment. I am only going to take my hat off.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: In his most earnest manner .
Oh! please don’t. It is so pretty. One of the prettiest hats I ever saw. I hope the Woman’s Liberal Association received it with loud applause.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: With a smile .
We have much more important work to do than look at each other’s bonnets, Lord Goring.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Really? What sort of work?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Oh! dull, useful, delightful things, Factory Acts, Female Inspectors, the Eight Hours’ Bill, the Parliamentary Franchise. . . . Everything, in fact, that you would find thoroughly uninteresting.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: And never bonnets?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: With mock indignation .
Never bonnets, never!
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: LADY CHILTERN goes out through the door leading to her boudoir .
Takes LORD GORING’S hand .
You have been a good friend to me, Arthur, a thoroughly good friend.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: I don’t know that I have been able to do much for you, Robert, as yet. In fact, I have not been able to do anything for you, as far as I can see. I am thoroughly disappointed with myself.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: You have enabled me to tell you the truth. That is something. The truth has always stifled me.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Ah! the truth is a thing I get rid of as soon as possible! Bad habit, by the way. Makes one very unpopular at the club . . . with the older members. They call it being conceited. Perhaps it is.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: I would to God that I had been able to tell the truth . . . to live the truth. Ah! that is the great thing in life, to live the truth.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Sighs , and goes towards the door .
I’ll see you soon again, Arthur, shan’t I?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN
